Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,

  1
 closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 12pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be summarized
by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City Council and will
also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be recorded for
public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

  3
 Consent Calendar Items

Agenda Items 3, 4 and 5 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including Ordinances,
Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent Calendar,
individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion of these
items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific items be
removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members of the
public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three (3)
minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

  6
 Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

image  will be used as the base map for the plan sheets.

including  plans, specifications,  and estimates  (PS&E). Design efforts  will align with other segments  of Phase

  Roadway  pavement  rehabilitation.

  Concrete  flatwork  replacement  (curb E!i gutter,  sidewalks,  cross gutters,  and driveways)
  ADA curb ramp  upgrades.

  Striping  modifications.

  Assumptions:

  ADA curb ramp upgrades  will reference  standard  details;  no additional  custom  construction
  details will be developed.

  All designs will be consistent  with established  project  standards  for Phase IV.

   OVERVIEW

The City of South Gate ("City")  2015 Zoning  Code prohibits  new industrial  warehouse  development  over 15,000  SF.
Because of the City's prime  location  near Port of LA and Long Beach and the growth  of e-commerce,  the City's
industrial  land is in high demand.  Landowners  and developers  are looking  for opportunities  to site new warehouses  and
distribution centers in the City. City has a number of industrial zoned parcels that are suited for redevelopment,  but
there are questions as to what will be acceptable uses for this land in the future.

Currently  there are industrial  parcels in the City that are blighted  and underutilized.  Landowners  and businesses are
interested  in bringing  in industrial  land uses that include warehouse  operations,  as a way to renew their  parcels.
Industrial development  with warehouses can create opportunities  for landowners  and create jobs, but they can also
create negative impacts for the community.

The City Council  directed  staff to review options  for development  alternatives,  which  are discussed in this report.
Thus, Kosmont  Companies  ('4Kosmont")  was retained  by the City to research various  policies adopted  by select cities.
While  there  are a few cities that prohibit  new warehouses,  most create policies to generate  substantial  revenue from
new warehouses,  to offset traffic  and other  impacts, and help achieve a better  balance for both the business and
residential  communities.

SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION  OF  REMOTE  PARTICIPATION  OPTIONS  FOR  CITY
COUNCIL  AND COMMISSION  MEETINGS

PURPOSE:  To present the City Council  with infonnation  on virtual  platfonn  options  for public
participation at City Councill and Coinmission  meetings,  including  the costs involved  and factors
weighing in favor and against such use.

RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  Receive report and provide  direction.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  Preliminary  cost estimates for additional staffing  are $12,180  per year with
an annual Zoom subscription  costing approximately  $7,000 per year.

BACKGROUND:  The City Council  directed  the City Manager  to provide  infon'nation  detailing
the costs and impacts of bringing back a call-in  or virtual  participation  platform  feature  at City
Council and Commission  meetings.

Coini'nencing  in Marcl'i2020,  amid implementation  of COVID-19  restrictions,  the Governor  issued
various  executive  orders relaxing  in-person  participation  requirements  under the Brown  Act and
pen'nitting  cities  in California  to provide  remote  features  such as Zoom  for public  access  and
participation  at public  meetings.  These temporary  remote features were used by both members  of
the public  and elected  and appointed  officials  to attend  meetings  remotely.  As  COVID-19
restrictions  were relaxed  and eventually  lifted,  the Governor's  executive  orders ended, requiring
cities to comply  with  pre-COVID-19  Brown  Act requirements.  Thus, the use of remote  public
participation  platfori'ns  at public  agency meetings  became voluntary  rather than mandatory,  and
somewhat  extinct.  In fact, most cities in the region  have discontinued  remote  access and moved
back to in person meetings  like they existed prior to March 2020. In a review  of Gateway  Cities in
our region, 28 of the 32 cities had returned  to in-person  public  participation  attendance.  Only 4
have retained remote/zoom  call-in features.

Anecdotally,  there  are several  varied  reasons  why  cities  may have eliminated  remote  public
participation  platfori'ns  from public meetings.  Ai'nong those reasons are cost related issues. Virtual
meetings,  in which  members  of the public  are in person and appear remotely,  tend to consume

  1

  129
 more ti'i'ne. While  there is a clear benefit  to a com+'nunity  member  being able to participate  remotely
at apublic  meeting,  tliere is also arisk  of abuse of tecl'inologyplatforins  by those wishing  to disrupt
or delay  public  agency  proceedings.  It is difficult  to deten'nine  or limit  a public  speaker,  liaving
already  corni'nented  once,  from  subsequently  calling  back  in under  a different  alias to provide
additional  comi'nents.

Other  cities  have  simply  balanced  the interest  of encouraging  public  participation  by in person
attendance  against  more  anonymous  and perhaps  less transparent  and respectful  call-in  or virtual
attendance.  There  are also balances  tliat have compared  the ease of participation  against  the added
impact  of requiring  staff members  to attend longer  meetings,  only to be expected  to return  the next
day at 7 am to complete  a 10-hour  workday.  Certainly,  the trend  among  cities  appears  to be to
returntopre-COVIDl9requirementsundertheBrownAct.  Indeed,whiletheLegislaturerecently
amended  the Brown  Act,  those amendments  did not require  cities  to continue  providing  remote
access  at public  meetings.

As a further  sign of backing  away from remote  participation,  recent amendments  to the Brown  Act
under  Assembly  Bill  2302  have  limited  the ability  of elected  officials  to attend  city  council
meetings  remotely.  AB  2302 limits  the use of remote  features  for City  Council  members  to only
certain  circumstances,  mostly  health  related,  thus predominantly  mandating  in person  attendance
except  in rare circumstances.  For cities that meet two times per month  City Council  members  shall
not attend in a remote  fashion  more than a maximum  of 5 times per year, The only exception  is for
emergencies.  The Brown  Act does not place similar  restrictions  on remote  access as it pertains  to
the public.

The  City  Council  received  infon'nation  last  year  on  retaining  remote  call-in  features  and
determined  they would  cease providing  remote  access for cornrnent.  Instead,  they invested  in video
equipment  and added the live video  feature  to Council  and Commission  meetings.  Now  that video
equipment  is installed,  all City  Council  and Coini'nission  meetings  are viewable  online,  both live
and in recorded  fori'n.

A benefit  of remote  access for public  coinment  using  a Zoom  or similar  platfon'n  is that it provides
a way for corni'nents  to be received  from  public  members  wlio  are not physically  present  or able to
attend meetings.  Currently,  those who are unable  to attend in person can still participate  by sending
comments  ahead of the meeting  to be read into  the record  during  the meeting.  In this  fashion,
those not in attendance  are treated  in a material  similar  fashion  as is they were in person.

As stated above,  drawbacks  of providing  a Zoom  or call-in  feature  include  the cost of additional
staffing  that  would  need to be added  to handle  the calls  or Zoom  requests  as the Clerk  and
Commission  assistants  currently  are fully  tasked  with  existing  duties  that include  supporting  the
meeting,  timing  comments,  reading  email  comments,  ensuring  the  video  feed  is  operating
correctly,  and handling  presentations.  An estimate  of additional  labor  costs is $12,180  for staffing
to cover  all Council  and Comi'nission  meetings.  An  additional  cost if Zoom  was to be used for
remote  access is the approximately  $7,000  cost for a City  Zoom  license.

An additional  drawback  is due to problems  that can occur  with  connectivity  for either  Zoom  or a
call-in  feature  if the system  disconnects  as has happened  numerous  times  wlien  the City  did use

  2

  130
 Zoom  during  tlie implementation  of COVID  19 restrictions.  If the system disconnects  or audio
issues occur tliis could constitute  a situation  where it could require the meeting  to be stopped and
possibly canceled ifthe public lost tlieir ability  to co'inment remotely,  or if a public member feigned
that the coitu'nunication was lost.

Staff maintains  that tlie current approach  at the City strikes a sufficient  balance between  the need
to conduct  tl'ie city's  business while  still allowing  for public  coinment.  In fact, the City provides
far more opportunity  for the public  to corninent  on both agenda and non-agenda  items tliat what is
required  under the Brown  Act, or is permitted  in many other facilities.  For example, the City does
not limit  the number  of speakers or the aggregate time allocated  for public  comment.  It also does
not require  the public to fill out a card identifying  the agenda item in advance upon which  the
public  member  wishes to coinrnent.

Staff seeks 'further guidance from the City Council  on which direction  to consider, namely whether
to implement  a remote participation  option,  or to keep its current practice  in place without  further
change.
